input: The wall thickness of the reboiler, once the corrosion allowance has been added, is 72 mm. This figure represents the thickness that is required by the pressure calculation, together with the allowance for material that is lost to corrosion over the life of the vessel, and it is the thickness that will be carried on the fabrication drawings. The flanges that close the reboiler raise a separate question, namely the choice of gasket material, and the comparison that is made here is between two materials that are judged on the basis of temperature limit alone. On this criterion, the higher-rated material is preferred: the flange face is exposed to the full temperature of the vapour space, and a gasket whose limit sits close to the operating temperature has essentially no margin for the excursions that start-up and upset conditions can produce. The same two materials are also candidates at the flanges of the absorber, where the temperatures are set by the same solvent circuit, and the preference that is formed here carries over to that service unless a condition that is specific to the absorber changes it. However, what the temperature limit does not settle is behaviour over time: a gasket in the reboiler flange is heated and cooled as the unit is started and stopped, and the lean solvent pump, which circulates the solvent through the absorber and the reboiler in turn, imposes its own cycle of pressure on the joint at each start. Whether the higher-rated material will keep its seal through that cycling, at a wall and flange built to 72 mm, is the point that the comparison on temperature limit leaves open.
